U.S. drug czar McCaffrey´s response to Gingrich drug policy criticism

Countering congressional criticism of the Clinton administration’s approach to the drug problem, White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) Director Barry McCaffrey maintains that objective studies show that U.S. anti-drug policy is working.

"The National Household Survey on Drug Abuse is our best measure" and finds an overall decline in drug use, according to a statement by ONDCP April 30.

House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich issued a statement the same day offering what he called a new approach to ending drug abuse, "waged on three major fronts—deterring demand, stopping supply, and increasing accountability."

Gingrich says ONDCP has relied too much on data that show only some progress and has failed to meet "specific achievable targets."

Following is the text of the ONDCP statement:

NATION MAKING PROGRESS IN REDUCING DRUG USE AND CONSEQUENCES

We are beginning to see evidence that ground lost ever the past six years—particularly among kids—is being made up. The key surveys of America’s drug problem are the basis for this assertion.

CHILDREN

The University of Michigan’s annual Monitoring The Future Study is our best device for measuring juvenile attitudes towards drugs and drug usage patterns. The 1997 report found that:

OVERALL DRUG USE

The National Household Survey on Drug Abuse is our best measure of overall national drug trends. The 1997 survey reported that:

COCAINE

The Department of Justice Drug Use Forecasting Program which monitors drug use among arrestees confirms the nation’s crack epidemic continues to abate.

HEALTH CONSEQUENCES OF ILLEGAL DRUGS

The Department of Health and Human Services Drug Abuse Warning Network keeps track of drug-related hospital emergency room cases. The latest report which analyzed trends through 1996 found that:

SPENDING ON ILLEGAL DRUGS

Reflecting this reduction in overall drug use in America, we estimate that spending has dropped by a third from $91,000 million in 1988 to $57,000 million in 1995.

WHAT ARE OUR MAJOR CHALLENGES?

Here’s what we’ll be working on in a bipartisan manner:

 

PLAN OF ACTION IS THE 1998 NATIONAL DRUG CONTROL STRATEGY

Our long-term goal is to reduce illegal drug use by 50 percent over the next ten years. With full congressional support, we can reduce drug use from today’s level of 6 percent of the population to the lowest levels seen in the last 30 years.

We’ve submitted a record budget to the Congress. Thirty-five percent of new FY99 drug-control spending is for drug prevention.

This ten-year plan is balanced and comprehensive. It represents consultation with all members of Congress, the national Governors’ Association, the U.S. Conference of Mayors, law enforcement organizations, prevention experts, and treatment providers, academia, community anti-drug coalitions, chambers of commerce, non governmental organizations, and religious leaders.

We welcome a full debate of its goals and objectives and supporting initiatives. What we don’t welcome is finger pointing and pettiness for political gain. This problem is too serious to be treated as a political football.
